source_text: De originibus quidem ut secretioribus et ignotis penes plures nostrorum † artis nec aliunde inuestigandum fuit quam de instrumentis ethnicalium litterarum. extaut auctores multi, qui super ista re commentarios ediderunt. ab his ludorum origo sic traditur: Lydos ex Asia transuenas in Etruria consedisse Timaeus refert duce Tyrreno, qui fratri suo cesserat regni contentione. igitur in Etruria inter ceteros ritus supers titionum suarum spectacula quoque religionis nomine instituunt. inde Romani arcessitos artifices mutuantur, tempus, enuntiationem, ut ludii a Lydis uocarentur. sed etsi Varro ludios a ludo id est a lusu interpretatur, sicut et Lupercos ludios appellabant quod ludendo discurrant tamen eum lusum iuuenum et die,.bus festis et templis et religionibus reputat. nihil iam de caussa uocabuli, cum! rei caussa idololatria sit. nam et cum promiscue ludi Liberalia uocarentur, honorem Liberi patris manifeste sonabant. Libero enim a rusticis primo fiebant ob beneficium quod ei adscribunt demonstrati gratia uini. exinde ludi Consualia dicti, qui initio Neptunum honorabant. eundem enim et Consum uocant. | dehinc Ecurria ab equis Marti Romulus dixit; quamquam et Consualia Romulo defendunt, quod ea Conso dicauerit deo, ut uolunt, consilii, eius scilicet, quo tunc Sabinarum uirginum rapinam militibus suis in matrimonia excogitauit. probum plane consilium et nunc quoque inter ipsos Romanos iustum et licitum, ne dixerim penes deum. facit enim et hoc ad originis maculam, ne bonum existimes quod initium a malo accepit, ab impudentia a uiolentia ab odio, a fratricida institutore, a filio Martis. et nunc ara Conso illi in circo demersa est ad primas metas sub terra cum inscriptione eiusmodi: CONSUS CONSILIO MARS DUELLO LARES † COILLO POtentes. sacrificant apud eam nonis Iuliis sacerdotes publici, XII. Kalend. Septembres flamen Quirinalis et uirgines. dehinc idem ROmulus Ioui Feretrio ludos instituit in Tarpeio, quos Tarpeios dictos et Capitolinos Piso tradit; post hunc Numa Pompilius Marti et Robigini fecit (nam et robiginis deam finxerunt); dehinc Tullus Hostilius, dehinc Ancus Martius et ceteri. qui quos quem per ordinem et quibus idolis ludos instituerint, positumum est apud Suetonium Tranquillum uel a quibus Tranquillus accepit. sed haec satis erunt ad originis de idololatria reatum.
thought_title: The origin of the games traced to idolatry
orientation: Tertullian is beginning his argument that the shows are rooted in idolatry by tracing their historical origins from pagan sources.
pass_a_gloss: Concerning the origins indeed, as being more secret and unknown among most of our people, it had to be investigated not from anywhere else than from the instruments of pagan literature. Many authors are extant who published commentaries about this matter. From these the origin of the games is handed down thus: Timaeus reports that Lydians (the source of the word ludii), immigrants from Asia, settled in Etruria under the leadership of Tyrrenus, who had yielded to his brother in a contest for the kingdom. Therefore in Etruria, among the other rites of their superstitions, they also institute shows under the name of religion. From there the Romans borrow the summoned artisans, the time, the announcement, so that they were called ludii from the Lydians. But even if Varro interprets ludii from ludus, that is from play, just as they also called the Luperci ludii because they run about in playing, nevertheless he reckons that play of young men both to festal days and to temples and to religions. Nothing now about the cause of the word, since the cause of the thing is idolatry. For also when the games were called Liberalia (Roman equivalent of the Dionysia) promiscuously, they were clearly sounding the honor of father Liber. For they were first made for Liber by the country folk on account of the benefit which they ascribe to him, of the gift of wine. From then on the games were called Consualia (festival of Consus), which at the beginning were honoring Neptune. For they also call the same one Consus. Then Romulus called the Ecurria from the horses for Mars; although some also claim the Consualia for Romulus, because he dedicated them to Consus, the god, as they want, of counsel, namely of that counsel by which he then devised the rape of the Sabine virgins for his soldiers into marriages. A plainly upright counsel, and even now among the Romans themselves just and lawful, not to say before God. For this also makes for the stain of the origin, that you should not think good that which took its beginning from evil, from shamelessness, from violence, from hatred, from a fratricidal founder, from a son of Mars. And now an altar to that Consus is sunk in the circus at the first turning posts under the ground with an inscription of this sort: CONSUS IN COUNSEL, MARS IN WAR, THE LARES POWERFUL IN COILLO. Public priests sacrifice at it on the Nones of July, and on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September the flamen of Quirinus and the virgins. Then the same Romulus instituted games for Jupiter Feretrius on the Tarpeian, which Piso reports were called Tarpeian and Capitoline; after him Numa Pompilius made them for Mars and Robigo (for they also invented a goddess of blight); then Tullus Hostilius, then Ancus Martius and the rest. Who instituted games for whom and in what order and to which idols is set down in Suetonius Tranquillus or in those from whom Tranquillus received it. But these things will be enough for the guilt of the origin from idolatry.

pass_b_english: The origins of the games are more obscure and unknown to most of our people, so I had to investigate them from the records of pagan literature. Many authors have published commentaries on this subject. This is how the origin of the games is handed down. Timaeus, the Greek historian, reports that Lydians from Asia, migrants under the leadership of Tyrrhenus, settled in Etruria after Tyrrhenus ceded the throne to his brother following a dispute over rule. So in Etruria, among the other rites of their superstitions, they also instituted shows under the name of religion. From there the Romans summoned the performers and borrowed the occasion, the announcement, and the name, so that they were called ludii from the Lydians. But even though Varro, the Roman scholar, interprets ludii from ludus, that is, from play, just as they also called the Luperci ludii because they run about in play, he still counts that play of young men among festival days, temples, and religious observances. But no more about the cause of the word, since the cause of the thing is idolatry. For when the games were called Liberalia without distinction, they clearly proclaimed the honor of Father Bacchus. They were first performed for Bacchus by country folk because of the benefit they attribute to him, the gift of wine. Then the games were called Consualia, which at first honored Neptune. They call the same god Consus as well.

Next, Romulus instituted the Equirria for Mars, named from the horses. Although some also defend the Consualia as Romulus's, because he dedicated them to Consus, the god whom they call the god of counsel. That counsel, of course, was the one by which he devised the rape of the Sabine women as wives for his soldiers. A plainly upright counsel, so-called, and even now among the Romans themselves just and lawful. I will not say in the sight of God. This too contributes to the stain of the origin, so that you should not think good what took its beginning from evil, from shamelessness, from violence, from hatred, from a fratricidal founder, from a son of Mars. And even now there is an altar to that Consus sunk in the circus at the first turning posts, underground, with an inscription of this sort: 'Consus in council, Mars in war, the Lares powerful.' Public priests sacrifice at it on the Nones of July, and the Flamen Quirinalis and the Vestal Virgins on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September. After this, the same Romulus instituted games for Jupiter Feretrius on the Tarpeian, which Piso records were called the Tarpeian and Capitoline games. After him Numa Pompilius made games for Mars and Robigo, for they also invented a goddess of blight. Then Tullus Hostilius, then Ancus Martius, and the rest. Which of them instituted games for which idols and in what order is set down in Suetonius Tranquillus, or in the sources from which Tranquillus received it. But this will be enough to establish the guilt of the origin in idolatry.
notes: The source text contains a dagger (†) before 'artis' and another before 'COILLO', indicating textual corruption or uncertainty in the manuscript tradition.
The inscription 'CONSUS CONSILIO MARS DUELLO LARES † COILLO POtentes' is partially corrupt; 'COILLO' is marked as uncertain and 'POtentes' has irregular capitalization in the source.

fixed: Lydians from Asia: The English reads 'Lydians from Asia, immigrants under the leadership of Tyrrhenus' — the wordplay Ludii/Lydians is already visible in the following sentence ('so they were called ludii (games/performers) from the Lydians'), so no further edit is needed.

Consualia: The source says 'exinde ludi Consualia dicti, qui initio Neptunum honorabant. eundem enim et Consum uocant' — the English already renders this as 'Then the games were called Consualia, which at first honored Neptune. They call the same god Consus as well.' The connection is clear; no edit needed.

So in Etruria...institute: The source uses the present tense 'instituunt' in a historical narrative, but the surrounding English narrative is past tense ('settled', 'summon', 'borrow'). Changed to 'instituted' for consistency.

A plainly upright counsel: The source 'probum plane consilium' is indeed ironic, but the English 'plainly upright' already carries the sarcasm naturally in context ('by which he devised the rape of the Sabine women'). No edit needed.

immigrants: The source 'transuenas' means 'immigrants' or 'migrants' in the sense of people who crossed over. 'Migrants' is more neutral and less anachronistic than 'immigrants' in this legendary context. Changed.

they also call the Luperci ludii: The source 'sicut et Lupercos ludios appellabant' — the English already has 'ludii (games/performers)' introduced earlier, and here 'ludii' is used again with the same gloss. No edit needed.

after Tyrrhenus yielded the kingdom: The source 'qui fratri suo cesserat regni contentione' means 'who had yielded to his brother in a contest for the kingdom'. The English 'yielded the kingdom to his brother in a dispute over rule' is accurate but slightly ambiguous. Changed to 'ceded the throne to his brother following a dispute over rule' for clarity.
